purpose: Teach evaluation and observability as a continuing evidence process that tests answer and task quality, source coverage, tool correctness, trajectory, policy behavior, refusal, recovery, drift, latency, cost, and human-review effort.
staffSummary: Build M24 around one consequential utility situation and one decision: Define the test set, signals, metrics, thresholds, reviewers, incident response, regression checks, correction action, and stop rule for a utility artificial intelligence or agent system. The learner must leave with a usable agent evaluation, observability, and continuing-assurance plan, not a collection of definitions.
openingSituation: A source-grounded assistant answers common questions well but fails on outdated procedures, conflicting documents, and questions outside its permission boundary.
learnerDecision: Define the test set, signals, metrics, thresholds, reviewers, incident response, regression checks, correction action, and stop rule for a utility artificial intelligence or agent system.
analogy: A laboratory does not trust one clean sample. It uses controls, known cases, repeats, limits, and corrective action. AI evaluation needs the same discipline.
learnerOutcomes: Explain Evals: How You Measure Whether It Works in plain English and connect it to a real water, wastewater, stormwater, or One Water decision.

Distinguish test case, task outcome, groundedness, source coverage, tool correctness, trajectory, metric, signal, trace, threshold, benchmark, drift, incident, acceptance, and continuing assurance without using one term to hide several different jobs.
Analyze the module situation, identify missing evidence, and name the professional consequence of a weak decision.
Compare how the same question changes across drinking water, wastewater, stormwater, administration, engineering, finance, technology, and public leadership.

Evaluate sources, assumptions, limitations, permissions, and human authority using this boundary: A benchmark, dashboard, average score, missing alert, or one successful demonstration does not prove utility fitness, safety, fairness, compliance, or performance under changed conditions.
Create a usable agent evaluation, observability, and continuing-assurance plan with evidence, roles, limits, review steps, and the next accountable action.
Defend the recommendation to Foundation, Practitioner, and Leader audiences while keeping disagreement and uncertainty visible.
curriculumOutcomes: Give Evals: How You Measure Whether It Works one clear learning job inside Governance, Security and Provenance.
Connect the module to a consequential decision and the agent evaluation, observability, and continuing-assurance plan.
Preserve current content, proposals, enhancements, and contributor records by stable identifier.
Separate verified evidence, Hardeep positions, expert interpretation, instructional scenarios, and unresolved questions.
Create an explicit bridge to the preceding and following modules without duplicating their work.
marketingOutcomes: Describe the practical value as helping a learner make and explain this decision: Define the test set, signals, metrics, thresholds, reviewers, incident response, regression checks, correction action, and stop rule for a utility artificial intelligence or agent system.
Name the agent evaluation, observability, and continuing-assurance plan as the visible result of the module.
Do not promise savings, compliance, certification, safety, performance, implementation success, or career outcomes without separately approved evidence.
requiredWorkProduct: agent evaluation, observability, and continuing-assurance plan
definitionOfDone: The learner explains the core distinctions, completes the required evidence and decision activities, passes distributed checks, saves a complete agent evaluation, observability, and continuing-assurance plan, and names the next accountable action.
scopeBoundary: A benchmark, dashboard, average score, missing alert, or one successful demonstration does not prove utility fitness, safety, fairness, compliance, or performance under changed conditions.
researchQuestions: What must an intelligent newcomer understand about Evals: How You Measure Whether It Works before using it in utility work?

Which sources can support the distinctions among test case, task outcome, groundedness, source coverage, tool correctness, trajectory, metric, signal, trace, threshold, benchmark, drift, incident, acceptance, and continuing assurance?

What evidence would allow a practitioner to make this decision: Define the test set, signals, metrics, thresholds, reviewers, incident response, regression checks, correction action, and stop rule for a utility artificial intelligence or agent system.
Which failure modes, counterexamples, and edge conditions could make the agent evaluation, observability, and continuing-assurance plan misleading?
How does the question change across drinking water, wastewater, stormwater, reuse, finance, engineering, administration, technology, and public accountability?
Which actions require qualified operator, engineer, water-quality, cybersecurity, privacy, legal, procurement, records, finance, accessibility, or executive review?

Which claims remain outside the module boundary: A benchmark, dashboard, average score, missing alert, or one successful demonstration does not prove utility fitness, safety, fairness, compliance, or performance under changed conditions.

acceptedExpansions.title: Agent-specific evaluation and continuous assurance
acceptedExpansions.recommendation: Extend evaluation from answer quality to the complete agent trajectory, including task result, tool use, source coverage, policy behavior, recovery, latency, cost, and human-review effort.
acceptedExpansions.description: Extend evaluation from answer quality to the complete agent trajectory, including task result, tool use, source coverage, policy behavior, recovery, latency, cost, and human-review effort.
learningObjectives: Define task success and failure before selecting an agent metric.
Evaluate answer quality, groundedness, source coverage, tool-call correctness, trajectory, refusal, recovery, latency, cost, and human effort.
Build a representative test set with ordinary, boundary, adversarial, stale, conflicting, and failure cases.
Set acceptance thresholds, stop rules, regression tests, reviewers, and correction actions.
Create an agent evaluation and continuing-assurance plan.
acceptedExpansions.evidenceBoundary: An average score or one successful demonstration does not prove fitness for a utility task, safety, fairness, compliance, or performance under changed conditions.

acceptedExpansions.title: Observability, drift, degradation, and incident response
acceptedExpansions.recommendation: Teach how a team notices that data, sources, model behavior, prompts, tools, permissions, infrastructure, cost, or human work has changed, then pauses, investigates, corrects, and records the response.
acceptedExpansions.description: Teach how a team notices that data, sources, model behavior, prompts, tools, permissions, infrastructure, cost, or human work has changed, then pauses, investigates, corrects, and records the response.
learningObjectives: Explain observability as the evidence needed to understand a changing system, not as a dashboard alone.
Distinguish data drift, concept drift, model degradation, retrieval staleness, prompt regression, tool failure, permission change, and workflow change.
Select signals, logs, traces, thresholds, alerts, owners, and response times for one utility application.
Investigate an incident without overwriting prior evidence and decide whether to continue, restrict, roll back, or stop.
Create an artificial intelligence observability and incident-response record.
acceptedExpansions.evidenceBoundary: A missing alert does not prove a system is healthy. Monitoring scope, blind spots, retention, privacy, and responsible human response must remain visible.

subtopics.title: Signals, logs, traces, measures, alerts, and ownership
